mentions.name: Larm
mentions.description: An uptime monitoring service with global probe coverage, automatic and standalone status pages, and many alert channels, offering simple pricing and generous limits. It runs on an Elixir backend with a worldwide network of small Go probes connected by TCP tunnels, stores check result data in ClickHouse, generates status pages on demand served through a CDN, and is EU hosted.
mentions.source_excerpt: I've recently been making improvements to Larm, https://larm.dev, an uptime monitoring service I've been running for a while now. It's got global probe coverage, automatic/standalone status pages, and lots of alert channels.
mentions.author: shintoist

mentions.name: larm.dev
mentions.description: Uptime monitoring service built in Elixir with a Phoenix LiveView dashboard. Runs a distributed cluster of three nodes communicating with each other, with tiny Go probe binaries spread across hosting providers worldwide to check monitoring targets, plus synthetic probes running in Playwright sandboxes. Stores large volumes of monitoring events in ClickHouse and handles work distribution strategies for both basic TCP/HTTP probes and synthetic workers.
mentions.problem: Uptime monitoring is a crowded field with new apps appearing almost daily, making it hard to effectively stand out in the noise.
mentions.source_excerpt: I'm building an uptime monitoring service, in Elixir, called https://larm.dev. It's a tough field because for some reason people vibe coding apps think this is very easy to do, and there are new apps coming out pretty much every day.
mentions.author: shintoist
